newsitem.title: INDIA: Amnesty urges end to Afghan human rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges end to Afghan human rights abuses.

text.p: Amnesty International's Indian unit on Saturday criticised the killing of former Afghan president Najibullah by Taleban militia and called on governments to stop human rights abuses in Afganistan.

"The manner in which Dr Najibullah was killed defies all norms of international law," S.S. Nehra, president of the Indian section of London-based Amnesty International, said in a statement released in the Indian capital.
"These latest events should surely provide the impetus for those governments with influence in the region to stop the massive human rights abuses perpetrated on the Afghan people."
Najibullah was taken out of a U.N. compound in the Afghan capital Kabul, shot in the head and hung on a tower by Taleban militia on Friday after their forces overran the city.
The Amnesty statement said the Taleban "have been responsible for the killing of hundreds of innocent people in indiscriminate rocket attacks against residential areas in and around Kabul".
It said Taleban leaders had frequently ordered the execution of suspected opponents, and that civilians in areas already taken over by the Taleban have been denied basic and fundamental human rights.

In some of the first measures enforced after taking control of Kabul, the Taleban barred women from offices until further orders and asked them to wear the traditional Islamic "hejab" veil when outside their homes.
Religious scholar Mullah Agha Gulabi said on official Kabul Radio that adulterers and drinkers must be killed.
Amnesty's Indian unit said the Taleban had introduced stoning and amputation in areas they had taken over.
It said that in a report released less than a year ago, Amnesty International revealed a pattern of human rights abuses by all sides in the armed conflict.

"Regional governments have denied involvement in recent developments in Afghanistan affairs," the statement said. "Nevertheless, it is clear that some governments can, and should exert influence on the warring factions."
The statement said the telephone system in Kandahar and other Taleban-controlled areas was part of the Pakistan telephone exchange system.

"Surely, if Pakistan and the Taleban can cooperate on strategically important areas such as telecommunications, the Pakistan government is in a strong position to help promote and protect human rights in Afghanistan," it said.

Pakistan appeared to signal its recognition on Friday of the new Taleban militia government in neighbouring Afghanistan, announcing that it would send a delegation to establish contact with "the new government in Kabul".

Pakistan's priority would be "to impress upon the new government the need for restraint and for maintenance of conditions for the unimpeded flow of humanitarian assistance to the population of Kabul," a Pakistan government statement said.
"It will also urge the need for such dialogue as may promote peace in all areas of Afghanistan," the statement said.
